builder_plan.scenario: An assistant chooses the wrong API or sends arguments your product cannot use.
builder_plan.change: Apply the proposed tool-selection or argument-generation change in a sandbox.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current agent with the same tool schemas and task budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct completed actions, invalid calls, retries, latency, and cost per completed task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction
summary: SimRec replaces hand-designed recommendation workflows and component-wise training (query rewriting, list ranking) with end-to-end GRPO reinforcement learning over the full interaction trajectory, using a task-anchored user simulator and a trajectory-level reward with training-only target injection. The cost is a full RL training pipeline: a user simulator (external LLM or self-play), reward engineering across retrieval quality, tool validity, and final hit, and GRPO rollouts, which exceeds inference-only constrained setups in compute and engineering complexity though the resulting 4B model itself fits a 24 GB GPU. It can fail when the simulated user's feedback distribution diverges from real users, when target injection biases the policy toward synthetic shortcuts, or when the reward does not transfer to catalogs and query distributions beyond ESCI and Amazon C4.
rationale: The method is relevant for teams shipping tool-using recommendation or search agents on small models, but its gains are demonstrated only on two benchmarks with simulated feedback, so production adoption requires validating the simulator-reward loop against real interaction data first.
technique: RL training of tool-integrated recommendation agents

claims.statement: SimRec replaces hand-designed recommendation workflows and component-wise training (query rewriting, list ranking) with end-to-end GRPO reinforcement learning over the full interaction trajectory, using a task-anchored user simulator and a trajectory-level reward with training-only target injection. The cost is a full RL training pipeline: a user simulator (external LLM or self-play), reward engineering across retrieval quality, tool validity, and final hit, and GRPO rollouts, which exceeds inference-only constrained setups in compute and engineering complexity though the resulting 4B model itself fits a 24 GB GPU. It can fail when the simulated user's feedback distribution diverges from real users, when target injection biases the policy toward synthetic shortcuts, or when the reward does not transfer to catalogs and query distributions beyond ESCI and Amazon C4.
SimRec improves NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% on ESCI and from 22.94% to 24.72% on Amazon C4, outperforming training-free agents on larger backbones.
